analysis.one_liner: Restores overtime pay for millions of salaried workers by raising and updating the exemption salary threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote; 57 House Democrats backed it and no Republican did.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, salaried workers labeled 'executive, administrative, or professional' can be denied overtime pay, no matter how little they earn, if their salary is above a threshold that had been frozen at $23,660 a year. This bill would write into law the Obama-era 2016 rule that raised that threshold to the 40th percentile of salaried earnings in the lowest-wage region — about $47,476 — making roughly 4.2 million additional workers eligible for overtime and strengthening protections for 8.9 million more, and it would automatically update the threshold every three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between the old threshold and the new one: they either gain overtime pay for hours over 40, or their employers must raise their salaries to keep them exempt. The bill text cites Department of Labor analysis that the underlying rule would benefit more than 13 million employees, including 4.2 million newly eligible.

how_it_helps.text: Writes the 2016 Labor Department threshold ($913/week, $47,476/year) into the Fair Labor Standards Act, protecting it from court challenge and repeal by later administrations.
Extends overtime pay eligibility to 4.2 million additional workers and strengthens protections for 8.9 million more, according to the bill's findings quoting the Labor Department.
Requires automatic updates to the threshold every three years based on wage data, without needing a new rulemaking, ending the pattern where the threshold went unraised for years and eroded in value.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried workers earning roughly $23,660 to $47,476 — including retail, restaurant, insurance, banking and nonprofit employers — who must either pay overtime or raise salaries. Some of that cost may be passed on through prices or reduced hours.

drawbacks.text: Employers bear real cost: for workers between the old and new thresholds, businesses must pay time-and-a-half for hours over 40 or raise salaries to keep them exempt, a burden falling hardest on smaller firms and sectors like retail and food service with long scheduling hours.

The bill locks the 2016 rule's one-size-fits-all 40th-percentile formula into statute, removing future administrations' flexibility to set a lower threshold based on regional cost differences or economic conditions; the same district court that enjoined the rule had ruled the agency lacked authority to set the threshold at that level.
Some employers respond to higher overtime costs by converting salaried positions to hourly with limited scheduling, or cutting base pay and hours, so not every affected worker comes out ahead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most workers near the threshold, overtime rights are a large and direct gain, and the 2016 rulemaking processed 270,000 public comments before settling on a measured figure. The main honest objection is the fixed statutory formula: it removes the flexibility a future rulemaking would have to adjust for economic conditions, and compliance costs are genuine for labor-intensive employers. On balance, the benefit to millions of workers outweighs the compliance burden, though the rigid automatic update is a legitimate design concern.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress; the committee never held a hearing or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 30, 2017 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was ever recorded; the Congress ended January 3, 2019 with the bill still in committee, never reaching a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
Its 57 cosponsors were all House Democrats; the House was under Republican majority control during the entire 115th Congress.

The bill responded to a federal district court in Texas enjoining and then invalidating the 2016 overtime rule, which the bill's findings described as threatening overtime protections for millions of workers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of salaried workers earning between roughly $23,660 and $47,476 kept them exempt from overtime without paying higher wages, and the Education and Workforce Committee majority avoided a vote that would have put overtime expansion on the record. Workers in that salary band lost the overtime rights the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers kept overtime exemptions; committee majority avoided a vote

for.name: Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 57 cosponsors, all fellow Democrats, to codify the 2016 overtime rule into statute.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or floor consideration during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.role: Employer trade associations opposed to the 2016 overtime rule
against.what_they_did: Opposed and litigated against the underlying 2016 overtime rule the bill would codify, culminating in the district court injunction and invalidation the bill's findings describe.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the House Committee on Education and the Workforce had a Republican majority that took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Employers of salaried workers (retail, restaurants, insurance, banking, nonprofits)
industries.note: These employers would have had to pay time-and-a-half for overtime hours worked by salaried staff earning up to about $47,476, or raise their salaries to keep them exempt. Blocking the bill preserved the $23,660 exemption threshold, keeping millions of salaried workers working extra hours without overtime pay.

Automatic triennial updates written into statute would have simplified compliance versus recurring rulemaking battles, but the higher threshold and reclassification of millions of workers would have generated significant new compliance and payroll-adjustment demand. Secondary effect either way.
